The CDC continues to update its list of symptoms as they learn more about the virus.

related_questions.question: Why does my nose run like water?

text_blocks.snippet: A runny nose that is clear and watery can be caused by a variety of factors, including allergies, colds, and even certain medical conditions like vasomotor rhinitis. While it often resolves on its own, especially if it's due to a cold, persistent or severe cases may require medical attention.
snippet_highlighted_words: can be caused by a variety of factors, including allergies, colds, and even certain medical conditions like vasomotor rhinitis

list.title: Allergies:
list.snippet: Allergens like pollen, dust, or pet dander can irritate the nasal passages and trigger a runny nose.

list.title: Colds and Flu:
list.snippet: Viral infections like the common cold or flu can cause inflammation and increased mucus production, leading to a runny nose.

list.title: Vasomotor Rhinitis:
list.snippet: This condition involves a miscommunication between the brain and nasal passages, causing them to react to triggers like temperature changes, spicy foods, or pollution by producing excessive mucus.

list.title: Lasting more than a week:
list.snippet: If your runny nose persists for more than a week, it's a good idea to consult with a doctor to rule out other potential causes.

list.title: Accompanying other symptoms:
list.snippet: If you experience fever, nausea, vomiting, or pain alongside a runny nose, it's recommended to see a doctor.

list.title: Head injury:
list.snippet: If your runny nose follows a head injury, especially if the discharge is clear and watery, it could indicate a cerebrospinal fluid leak (a serious condition) and requires immediate medical attention.

list.title: One-sided discharge:
list.snippet: If the runny nose is only from one nostril and especially if it's foul-smelling or bloody, seek medical advice promptly.

list.title: Difficulty breathing or swelling:
list.snippet: If you experience difficulty breathing or swelling in your forehead, eyes, side of your nose, or cheek, consult a doctor immediately.
Stay hydrated: Drinking plenty of fluids can help thin the mucus and relieve congestion.
Rest: Getting enough sleep allows your body to repair itself and fight off infection.
Use soft tissues: Opt for soft tissues to avoid irritating your nose.
Warm compresses: Applying a warm compress to your face can help relieve sinus pressure and congestion.
Saline nasal spray: Using a saline spray can help to rinse out your nasal passages and moisturize them.
Steam inhalation: Inhaling steam from a bowl of hot water or a shower can help loosen congestion.
